tldr: By formulating local swarm interactions as energies in a Gibbs random field and mapping them directly to structured reinforcement learning rewards, the authors propose a single decentralized swarm control framework adaptable to diverse missions without retraining. Through simulations and real-world flights, they demonstrate zero-shot transfer of the same policy across tasks ranging from formation flight and high-speed racing to area exploration.
hero_caption: Overview of swarm control via probabilistic energy modeling. Inspired by flocks of birds and schools of fish, relations with the environment (one-body terms) and between drones (two-body terms) are formulated as Gibbs energies, tying energy minimization directly to reinforcement learning reward maximization. Trained policies are combined via a lightweight policy gating network, enabling zero-shot transfer across varied tasks and physical hardware platforms without retraining.
overview:
Swarms of multiple coordinating drones are expected to handle diverse applications such as exploration and surveillance. However, conventional control methods are typically tailored to individual tasks, such as maintaining a specific formation or navigating around obstacles. Every time mission objectives change, engineers must manually retune rules or redesign reinforcement learning reward functions and retrain policies from scratch.

To address this, the authors drew inspiration from biological swarms, which generate rich, collective behaviors from simple local interaction rules. Introducing Gibbs random fields (GRFs) from statistical mechanics, they realized that core swarm rules—cohesion, collision avoidance, and velocity matching—can all be expressed as energy terms. Minimizing this energy is mathematically equivalent to maximizing a structured reward in reinforcement learning. Instead of designing ad-hoc rewards for every task, any mission can be represented simply by weighting shared energy terms.

Evaluations spanned large-scale simulations with 10 to 100 agents as well as physical experiments using both 29 g ultra-compact Crazyflie drones and custom, larger outdoor drones. A single unified controller successfully handled six fundamentally different mission classes—narrow gate traversal, high-speed racing, patrol surveillance, pattern formation, and dispersed exploration—without any policy retraining.

The framework maintained high task success rates of 0.96–1.00 even in cluttered environments, achieving real-time inference latency of 1–10 ms per agent independent of swarm size. Furthermore, it demonstrated successful zero-shot transfer to novel indoor settings and GPS-denied woodland environments, establishing its practical utility as a foundational representation for swarm control.
contributions: Unifying swarm interaction rules into shared energy terms by exploiting the correspondence between Gibbs random field energy minimization and structured reinforcement learning reward maximization.

Deriving a theoretical decoupling framework that approximates global optimal configurations using only local observations, keeping computational complexity to $O(1)$ (1–10 ms) independent of swarm size.
Enabling instant switching across six distinct mission classes without retraining by combining pre-trained specialized policies through a lightweight gating network.
Demonstrating zero-shot transfer across physical scales and domains—from micro-drones to large outdoor platforms, and from indoor spaces to GPS-denied forests—via dimensionless normalization.

sections.heading: Why did drone swarm controllers need to be rebuilt for every task?
sections.summary: Existing swarm robotics controllers based on rules, optimization (MPC), or reinforcement learning are mostly tailored to single tasks, requiring retuning or retraining when missions change. This paper aims to discover a shared mathematical representation that unifies diverse swarm behaviors, achieving real-time, reusable decentralized policies.
sections.details:
Flocks of birds and schools of fish seamlessly switch between maintaining group cohesion, foraging, and navigational transit using only simple interactions between individuals. Robotics researchers have long pursued this capability, yet real-world robotic swarms often end up with single-purpose controllers dedicated exclusively to formation maintenance or obstacle avoidance. This stems from deep-seated trade-offs in existing paradigms:

- Rule-based methods (such as artificial potential fields): Computationally lightweight and suited for decentralized execution, but reliant on heuristic tuning and prone to getting stuck in unforeseen situations.
- Optimization-based methods (such as decentralized MPC): Capable of handling safety and robot dynamics rigorously, but exchanging trajectories and solving real-time optimizations between agents imposes prohibitive computational burdens on resource-constrained micro-drones.
- Deep reinforcement learning (MARL): Allows fast on-board inference by offloading computational burdens to offline training, but reward functions are handcrafted for individual tasks, requiring retraining or new dedicated models whenever new missions arise.

In short, the field lacked a foundational representation that simultaneously provides swarm versatility, real-time computation, and cross-task reusability. To bridge this gap, the authors turned to Gibbs random fields from statistical mechanics. By formulating environmental relationships (one-body terms) and inter-robot interactions (two-body terms) as reusable energy terms, they developed a unified controller capable of executing diverse missions without retraining.

sections.heading: Diverse missions and autonomous swarm behaviors achieved with a single unified policy
sections.summary: The proposed unified policy handles basic behaviors like cohesion and velocity tracking, as well as indoor high-speed racing, patrol, letter formations, and autonomous exploration in degraded environments without retraining. It achieved success rates of 0.96–1.00 in large-scale simulations, while real-world flights demonstrated zero-shot transfer to unknown forests and different hardware platforms.
sections.details:
### Method overview
Each robot is treated as a random variable, modeling the joint distribution of the entire system via a Gibbs energy $H(X)$. Because lower energy corresponds to a more desirable state, setting the reward to $R = -H(X)$ directly connects it to reinforcement learning. Using a decoupling theory that derives global optimal configurations from local observations alongside an action-attention mechanism, the controller weights the behavioral intentions of neighbors to achieve an $O(1)$ inference speed (1–10 ms) independent of swarm size. Mission switching is accomplished without any retraining by combining frozen specialized policies using a lightweight gating network.

### Elementary behaviors in simple scenarios
Closed-loop fundamental behaviors were evaluated first. The swarm rapidly adapted to sharp step changes in target inter-agent distance $d_{\mathrm{ref}}$ while keeping distance standard deviation below 0.5 m. It also tracked circular velocity commands with a 1.7 m radius without phase lag. When an obstacle appeared in its path, the swarm autonomously split into two groups to avoid it and rejoined afterward. The minimum clearance stayed above 0.25 m, well exceeding the 0.1 m safety margin.

### Versatile swarm control across missions
The same pre-trained policy was deployed across multiple distinct task classes:
- Traversal and racing: During narrow gate traversal, the swarm reduced its order parameter $\phi$ to deform flexibly, regaining alignment immediately after passing through. In high-speed racing, it accelerated up to 2 m/s on straights and decelerated to around 0.8 m/s in sharp turns, stretching into a ribbon-like longitudinal formation to clear gates at speed.
- Patrol and pattern formation: In patrol missions where environmental information decays over time, the swarm autonomously split into two subgroups, maintaining an average idle time of 2–3 s and a mean revisit interval of 6.6 s, keeping regional uncertainty low at 0.1–0.2. In a 16-drone letter formation task (S-Y-S-U), the swarm morphed smoothly into each letter shape within 40 s without deadlocks.
- Dispersed exploration and fault tolerance: In unknown area exploration, the remaining drones promptly redistributed themselves when individual units failed mid-mission. The swarm achieved 97.7% coverage with 8 functional drones, 98.2% even when one drone dropped out per squad, and 91.1% coverage with the surviving squad even after an entire sub-squad was completely lost.

### Benchmarking and interpreting local interactions
The framework was compared against baselines such as DMPC and potential fields in simulations with 10–100 agents and 10–50 obstacles. While conventional methods suffered sharp drops in success rate due to local minima or computational bottlenecks in cluttered environments, the proposed method maintained success rates of 0.96–1.00. Per-agent inference latency remained within 1–10 ms even as swarm size grew, and RMS acceleration stayed below 0.22 $\mathrm{m/s^2}$, yielding smooth trajectories. Furthermore, attention analysis revealed that agents attend not only to nearby neighbors, but also allocate high attention weights to agents with low time-to-collision (Inv-TTC), neighbors turning toward them, and neighbors facing acute obstacle collision risks.

### Zero-shot transfer across platforms and environments
Thanks to dimensionless normalization based on reference distance, the policy transferred seamlessly from 29 g Crazyflie drones to custom large outdoor drones without modifications. The swarm completed sophisticated physical missions zero-shot, including seamless transitions from an underground parking garage to outdoor spaces, flight through dense GPS-denied forests, and an exploration scenario where one drone stayed behind to monitor a detected target while the rest continued searching.

sections.heading: The future of swarm robotics unlocked by unified energy models, and remaining challenges
sections.summary: This work demonstrates that linking structured physical/statistical priors with deep reinforcement learning enables a single policy to generalize across diverse swarm behaviors. However, hurdles remain before real-world adoption, including reliance on local communication, behavior in non-convex boundaries, and 100-agent physical validations.
sections.details:
The core achievement of this paper is that formulating local swarm interactions as Gibbs energies provides a shared representation, shifting reinforcement learning policies from disposable, task-specific models into reusable, extensible modules. The attention-driven behavior where agents notice hazards threatening their peers qualitatively matches the global hazard awareness seen in natural swarms, offering an intriguing parallel.

Nonetheless, several limitations must be addressed for practical deployment:
- Theoretical safety guarantees: The framework assumes reliable neighbor communication and onboard state estimation. Rigorous collision avoidance guarantees under severe communication dropouts or heavy sensor noise are not yet established.
- Limitations of local sensing: Because agents rely strictly on local observations, there is an inherent risk of trapping in local minima within deeply labyrinthine, non-convex obstacle environments.
- Physical experimental scale: While simulation confirmed $O(1)$ computation up to 100 agents, real-world flight tests were limited to 16 agents. Deploying 100 physical drones simultaneously under real-world outdoor disturbances remains future work.

Moving forward, promising directions include integrating multimodal perception and extending the formulation to heterogeneous robot teams with diverse dynamic capabilities.

sections.heading: From Gibbs random fields to decentralized RL: Mathematical formulation and policy integration
sections.summary: The entire system is modeled as a Gibbs random field on an undirected graph, decoupling global energy into a form computable from local observations. Each agent is trained using attention-augmented PPO, and a unified controller is built by combining pre-trained specialized policies via a gating network.
sections.details:
### Probabilistic energy formulation
The configuration of the robotic swarm is treated as random variables on an undirected graph $\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})$, with joint distribution defined as $P(X) \propto \exp[-H(X)]$. The total energy $H(X)$ decomposes into one-body terms $\psi_i$ representing relations with the environment (target tracking, obstacle avoidance) and two-body terms $\psi_{ij}$ capturing inter-agent interactions (collision avoidance, velocity matching, cohesion). Since energy minimization corresponds to reward maximization, local rewards are formulated as $r_i = -(\psi_i + \frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}_i|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_i} \psi_{ij})$.
Crucially, directly computing the global pairwise energy $H_p$ locally would fail. Through mathematical proofs, the authors showed that a decoupled local pairwise energy $\hat{H}_p$, defined over neighbor sums, yields the exact same triangular lattice equilibrium as the global formulation. This guarantees that agents converge to globally optimal geometric configurations using purely local observations.

### Decentralized learning with attention
Each robot follows second-order equations of motion, utilizing a hybrid action space that pairs discrete acceleration vectors with braking heuristics. Because neighbor actions cannot be observed instantaneously, the previous action $\boldsymbol{A}_{j, t-1}$ is used as an intent proxy under a mean-field approximation.
To aggregate neighbor information, an action-attention mechanism computes queries, keys, and values from relative states between agents, calculating context-dependent weighted sums. Obstacles are perceived through a sector-partitioned LiDAR representation, and policies are trained via decentralized training decentralized execution (DTDE) with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO).
Furthermore, specialized policies pre-trained on individual tasks (such as traversal or racing) are frozen and blended by an integration module using a lightweight gating network $G_e(\boldsymbol{o}, \boldsymbol{c})$ conditioned on high-level mission commands and local observations. This architecture allows new specialized skills to be safely integrated over time without degrading existing capabilities.

takeaways: Mapping Gibbs energy minimization directly to structured reinforcement learning reward maximization allows diverse swarm task rewards to be expressed within a single unified representation.
Decoupled local energy formulation achieves global lattice equilibria using local information alone, maintaining $O(1)$ per-agent computation latency (1–10 ms) independent of swarm size.
Freezing specialized policies and combining them through a lightweight gating network enables multi-task swarm control while completely avoiding catastrophic forgetting and retraining costs.
Rigorous dimensionless normalization of the observation space enables zero-shot sim-to-real transfer as well as cross-platform deployment from micro-drones to large outdoor aircraft.
limitations: Requires reliable inter-agent communication and precise onboard state estimation, lacking formal safety guarantees (e.g., safety filters) under severe communication dropouts or sensor failures.
Relying on local observations and potential-based formulations leaves the swarm susceptible to local minima (deadlocks) in highly complex, non-convex obstacle environments.
Physical platform tests were capped at 16 drones; verifying whether the 100-agent scalability proven in simulation holds under real-world physical disturbances remains unverified.
